title: PersistBench: When Should Long-Term Memories Be Forgotten by LLMs?
claim: Persistent memory built from past sessions helps personalization but can leak into unrelated tasks or reinforce user biases.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right, curved arrows into a memory cloud, then two outputs
description: The figure has three columns, read left to right. On the left, two blue rounded panels show multi-session user–LLM chats, with chat bubbles, user icons and robot icons. In one session the user says they are vegan. In another the user mentions hypertension medication. Curved black arrows lead from these panels to a central robot with a thought-cloud labeled 'User memories', listing 'Is vegan' and 'Has hypertension'. Two arrows lead from the cloud to the right column. The top yellow panel is labeled 'Cross-domain leakage'. It shows a request for an email to a manager, and the assistant's reply wrongly mentions hypertension, with that word in red. The bottom green panel is labeled 'Sycophancy'. It shows the user asking whether a vegan diet is healthy, and the assistant answers that it is the 'healthiest', in red. Colored panels separate the stages.
caption: Persistent long-term memory is reused during inference in conversational assistants. While such memory enables personalization, it can also lead to cross-domain leakage and memory-induced sycophancy, which are evaluated in PersistBench.
abstract: Conversational assistants are increasingly integrating long-term memory with large language models (LLMs). This persistence of memories, e.g., the user is vegetarian, can enhance personalization in future conversations. However, the same persistence can also introduce safety risks that have been largely overlooked. Hence, we introduce PersistBench to measure the extent of these safety risks. We identify two long-term memory-specific risks: cross-domain leakage, where LLMs inappropriately inject context from the long-term memories; and memory-induced sycophancy, where stored long-term memories insidiously reinforce user biases. We evaluate 18 frontier and open-source LLMs on our benchmark. Our results reveal a surprisingly high failure rate across these LLMs - a median failure rate of 53% on cross-domain samples and 97% on sycophancy samples. To address this, our benchmark encourages the development of more robust and safer long-term memory usage in frontier conversational systems.
